claim: Multicellular organisms have evolved from a unicellular ancestor at least 25 times.
source: Multicellular organisms have evolved from a unicellular ancestor at least 25 times (Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007), but we know little about what selected for the simplest form of multicellularity: an undifferentiated clump of cells produced by the repeated division of a single cell.
evidence: Supported by citation to Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007

claim: Protection from predation, environmental stress, and phagocytosis has been proposed as a driving force for multicellularity.
source: Two driving forces have been proposed, protection from a variety of factors (including predation [Kessin et al., 1996], environmental stress [Smukalla et al., 2008], and phagocytosis [Boraas et al., 1998]) and more efficient nutrient usage (Dworkin, 1972; Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003; Koschwanez et al., 2011; Alegado et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kessin et al., 1996; Smukalla et al., 2008; and Boraas et al., 1998

claim: More efficient nutrient usage has been proposed as a driving force for multicellularity.
source: Two driving forces have been proposed, protection from a variety of factors (including predation [Kessin et al., 1996], environmental stress [Smukalla et al., 2008], and phagocytosis [Boraas et al., 1998]) and more efficient nutrient usage (Dworkin, 1972; Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003; Koschwanez et al., 2011; Alegado et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dworkin, 1972; Pfeiffer and Bonhoeffer, 2003; Koschwanez et al., 2011; Alegado et al., 2012

claim: Sharing public goods favors clumps over isolated cells.
source: In earlier work, we showed that sharing public goods favors clumps over isolated cells and proposed that sharing could have selected for simple multicellularity (Koschwanez et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Koschwanez et al., 2011)

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae utilizes sucrose by secreting invertase.
source: The budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, utilizes sucrose by secreting invertase (Dodyk and Rothstein, 1964; Carlson et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dodyk and Rothstein, 1964; Carlson et al., 1981

claim: Over 95% of invertase enzyme remains in the cell wall.
source: Over 95% of this enzyme remains in the cell wall (Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987), where it hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose, which are imported into the cell by a variety of hexose transporters (Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987

claim: Invertase hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose in the cell wall.
source: Over 95% of this enzyme remains in the cell wall (Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987), where it hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose, which are imported into the cell by a variety of hexose transporters (Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987; Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997

claim: Glucose and fructose are imported into yeast cells by a variety of hexose transporters.
source: Over 95% of this enzyme remains in the cell wall (Esmon et al., 1987; Tammi et al., 1987), where it hydrolyzes sucrose into glucose and fructose, which are imported into the cell by a variety of hexose transporters (Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meijer et al., 1996; Reifenberger et al., 1997

claim: Lab yeast strains cannot grow from low density in low concentrations of sucrose because of diffusion.
source: Lab yeast strains cannot grow from low density in low concentrations of sucrose because of diffusion: each cell captures only a small fraction of the sugars that sucrose hydrolysis releases, and the molecules released by other, distant cells are at very low concentration.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the physical properties of diffusion and the spatial distribution of cells

claim: Forming multicellular clumps overcomes the failure to grow in low sucrose concentrations.
source: Forming multicellular clumps overcomes this failure; cells in a clump can capture glucose and fructose diffusing from their neighbors and grow in concentrations of sucrose where low concentrations of individual cells cannot.
evidence: Based on inference from the spatial arrangement of cells in clumps and diffusion properties

claim: Three engineered strategies allow yeast cells to grow on low sucrose: forming multicellular clumps, importing sucrose before hydrolyzing it, and increasing invertase expression.
source: We engineered and tested three strategies that allow yeast cells to grow on low sucrose: forming multicellular clumps, importing sucrose before hydrolyzing it, and increasing invertase expression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2

claim: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from evolved populations

claim: Of 12 successful clones, 10 increased invertase expression.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNA sequencing

claim: None of the 12 successful clones imported sucrose.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from competition assays with suc2-1cyt strains

claim: Of 12 successful clones, 11 increased hexose transporter expression.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from RNA sequencing

claim: Increased hexose transporter expression was a strategy not anticipated by the researchers.
source: Of 12 successful clones, 11 formed multicellular clumps through incomplete cell separation, 10 increased invertase expression, none imported sucrose, and 11 increased hexose transporter expression, a strategy we had not engineered.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text

claim: Increasing invertase expression allows growth from a single cell in low sucrose concentrations.
source: Figure 2A shows that increasing invertase expression allows growth from a single cell in low sucrose concentrations; increasing inducer concentrations leads to better growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Increasing inducer concentrations leads to better growth in low sucrose.
source: Figure 2A shows that increasing invertase expression allows growth from a single cell in low sucrose concentrations; increasing inducer concentrations leads to better growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Mal11 is a maltose importer that can also import sucrose.
source: Mal11 is a maltose importer that can also import sucrose (Stambuk et al., 1999), but is not expressed in our yeast strains (Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stambuk et al., 1999

claim: Mal11 is not expressed in the lab yeast strains used in this study.
source: Mal11 is a maltose importer that can also import sucrose (Stambuk et al., 1999), but is not expressed in our yeast strains (Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2010

claim: SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains that make the maltose importer can grow from single cells on as little as 1 mM sucrose.
source: Figure 2B shows that both the SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains that make the maltose importer can grow from single cells on as little as 1 mM sucrose.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The importer makes extracellular sucrose digestion dispensable.
source: The nearly identical growth of the SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains shows that the importer makes extracellular sucrose digestion dispensable, and the failure of the suc2Δ strains to grow shows that sucrose utilization after import still requires invertase.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental data comparing SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains

claim: Sucrose utilization after import still requires invertase.
source: The nearly identical growth of the SUC2 and suc2-1cyt strains shows that the importer makes extracellular sucrose digestion dispensable, and the failure of the suc2Δ strains to grow shows that sucrose utilization after import still requires invertase.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing suc2Δ strains fail to grow

claim: The three engineered strains all outcompeted the ancestral wild-type lab strain in 1 mM sucrose.
source: The three engineered strains all outcompeted the ancestral wild-type lab strain in 1 mM sucrose (Table 1), although the strain engineered to express increased invertase (EngHiInvertase) was a much worse competitor than the other two (EngClumpy, EngSucImport).
evidence: Supported by competition data shown in Table 1

claim: The strain engineered to express increased invertase (EngHiInvertase) was a much worse competitor than EngClumpy and EngSucImport.
source: The three engineered strains all outcompeted the ancestral wild-type lab strain in 1 mM sucrose (Table 1), although the strain engineered to express increased invertase (EngHiInvertase) was a much worse competitor than the other two (EngClumpy, EngSucImport).
evidence: Supported by competition data shown in Table 1

claim: Ten independent populations of budding yeast were serially diluted in minimal, 1 mM sucrose-containing medium.
source: Ten independent populations of budding yeast were serially diluted in minimal, 1 mM sucrose-containing medium.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The starting strain for each population was a haploid, non-clumpy, prototrophic strain that constitutively expressed YFP and carried a DNA polymerase mutation (POL3-L523D) that elevated its mutation rate roughly 100-fold.
source: The starting strain for each population was a haploid, non-clumpy, prototrophic strain (Figure 3A) that constitutively expressed YFP and carried a DNA polymerase mutation (POL3-L523D) that elevated its mutation rate roughly 100-fold (Jin et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jin et al., 2005 and shown in Figure 3A

claim: Over 25–35 serial dilutions, the time it took the culture to become cloudy fell from 2 weeks to 3 days.
source: Over 25–35 serial dilutions, the time it took the culture to become cloudy fell from 2 weeks to 3 days, and all 10 populations (named EvoPopulation1–10) displayed a clumpy phenotype (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations during evolution

claim: All 10 evolved populations displayed a clumpy phenotype.
source: Over 25–35 serial dilutions, the time it took the culture to become cloudy fell from 2 weeks to 3 days, and all 10 populations (named EvoPopulation1–10) displayed a clumpy phenotype (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 3C

claim: Each of the evolved clones strongly outcompeted their ancestor, eliminating it from cultures within two passages on 1 mM sucrose.
source: Each of the evolved clones strongly outcompeted their ancestor, eliminating it from cultures within two passages on 1 mM sucrose (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by competition data shown in Table 1

claim: Efficient use of public goods, liberated through extracellular hydrolysis, selects for the evolution of undifferentiated multicellularity.
source: We conclude that efficient use of public goods, liberated through extracellular hydrolysis, selects for the evolution of undifferentiated multicellularity.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental evolution results

claim: Wild yeast isolates can form multicellular clumps through flocculation.
source: Wild yeast isolates can form multicellular clumps in two ways: flocculation (Guo et al., 2000), in which separate cells stick to each other via cell wall-bound adhesins, or failure to separate daughters from their mothers because the cell wall that joins them is not digested after cytokinesis (Yvert et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2000

claim: Wild yeast isolates can form multicellular clumps through failure to separate daughters from their mothers because the cell wall that joins them is not digested after cytokinesis.
source: Wild yeast isolates can form multicellular clumps in two ways: flocculation (Guo et al., 2000), in which separate cells stick to each other via cell wall-bound adhesins, or failure to separate daughters from their mothers because the cell wall that joins them is not digested after cytokinesis (Yvert et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yvert et al., 2003

claim: All the multicellular clones form clumps as a result of incomplete separation.
source: All the multicellular clones are the result of incomplete separation; each clump contains cells of only one or the other color.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from two-color fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Each clump contains cells of only one color, indicating incomplete separation rather than flocculation.
source: All the multicellular clones are the result of incomplete separation; each clump contains cells of only one or the other color.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from two-color fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: In 10 of the 12 clones invertase (SUC2) expression was elevated between 3- and 21-fold above their ancestor.
source: In 10 of the 12 clones invertase (SUC2) expression was elevated between 3- and 21-fold above their ancestor (Table 2); EvoClone7C and EvoClone8 were the only clones with no significant change in SUC2 expression.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Table 2

claim: EvoClone7C and EvoClone8 were the only clones with no significant change in SUC2 expression.
source: In 10 of the 12 clones invertase (SUC2) expression was elevated between 3- and 21-fold above their ancestor (Table 2); EvoClone7C and EvoClone8 were the only clones with no significant change in SUC2 expression.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Table 2

claim: ACE2 and UBR1 were mutated in at least half the clones.
source: Two genes, ACE2 and UBR1, were mutated in at least half the clones, and groups of genes in three pathways, involved in glucose sensing (the RGT1 group), growth regulation (the IRA1/IRA2 group), and transcription (the Mediator group) were also mutated in many clones.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing and bulk segregant analysis data shown in Table 5

claim: Groups of genes in three pathways involved in glucose sensing (the RGT1 group), growth regulation (the IRA1/IRA2 group), and transcription (the Mediator group) were mutated in many clones.
source: Two genes, ACE2 and UBR1, were mutated in at least half the clones, and groups of genes in three pathways, involved in glucose sensing (the RGT1 group), growth regulation (the IRA1/IRA2 group), and transcription (the Mediator group) were also mutated in many clones.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing and bulk segregant analysis data shown in Table 5

claim: Most of the putative causal mutations are likely loss of function mutations.
source: We suspect that most of the putative causal mutations are loss of function mutations.
evidence: Based on inference from the high frequency of nonsense mutations

claim: Ace2 activates the transcription of enzymes that degrade the septum that connects mother to daughter cell.
source: Ace2 activates the transcription of enzymes that degrade the septum that connects mother to daughter cell (Colman-Lerner et al., 2001; Sbia et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Colman-Lerner et al., 2001; Sbia et al., 2008

claim: ACE2 was mutated in eight evolved clones.
source: ACE2 was mutated in eight evolved clones; six of these mutations were nonsense mutations scattered through the open reading frame.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: Six of the ACE2 mutations were nonsense mutations scattered through the open reading frame.
source: ACE2 was mutated in eight evolved clones; six of these mutations were nonsense mutations scattered through the open reading frame.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: All six clones with ACE2 nonsense mutations had at least tenfold reductions in the expression of three genes known to aid in cell separation (CTS1, DSE1, and DSE2).
source: All six of these clones had at least tenfold reductions in the expression of three genes known to aid in cell separation (CTS1 [chitinase], DSE1, and DSE2 [supplementary file 1B]) in agreement with the original finding that ace2Δ mutants are clumpy (Dohrmann et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and citation to Dohrmann et al., 1992

claim: ace2Δ mutants are clumpy.
source: All six of these clones had at least tenfold reductions in the expression of three genes known to aid in cell separation (CTS1 [chitinase], DSE1, and DSE2 [supplementary file 1B]) in agreement with the original finding that ace2Δ mutants are clumpy (Dohrmann et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dohrmann et al., 1992

claim: Ubr1 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase in the N-end rule pathway.
source: Ubr1 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase in the N-end rule pathway. Ubr1 targets proteins with certain N-terminal amino acids, which are exposed by proteolytic cleavage or removal of the N-terminal methionine, for degradation (Bartel et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bartel et al., 1990

claim: UBR1 was mutated in 6 of the 12 clones.
source: UBR1 was mutated in 6 of the 12 clones; four mutations were nonsense mutations, strongly suggesting that the remaining two are also a loss of function mutations.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: Four UBR1 mutations were nonsense mutations.
source: UBR1 was mutated in 6 of the 12 clones; four mutations were nonsense mutations, strongly suggesting that the remaining two are also a loss of function mutations.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: Rad6 is the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme that forms a heterodimer with Ubr1.
source: Rad6, the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme that forms a heterodimer with Ubr1 (Dohmen et al., 1991), had a missense mutation in a seventh evolved clone.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dohmen et al., 1991

claim: Rad6 had a missense mutation in a seventh evolved clone.
source: Rad6, the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme that forms a heterodimer with Ubr1 (Dohmen et al., 1991), had a missense mutation in a seventh evolved clone.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: The Rgt1 pathway controls cells' response to external glucose concentrations.
source: The Rgt1 pathway controls cells' response to external glucose concentrations. In high glucose, Rgt1, a transcription factor, represses the expression of high affinity hexose transporters such as HXT4 (Ozcan and Johnston, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ozcan and Johnston, 1999

claim: In high glucose, Rgt1 represses the expression of high affinity hexose transporters such as HXT4.
source: In high glucose, Rgt1, a transcription factor, represses the expression of high affinity hexose transporters such as HXT4 (Ozcan and Johnston, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ozcan and Johnston, 1999

claim: In low glucose, Snf3 induces degradation of Mth1, a protein that is needed for Rgt1 to exert its repressive effects.
source: In low glucose, Snf3, a membrane-spanning glucose sensor, induces degradation of Mth1, a protein that is needed for Rgt1 to extert its repressive effects (Broach, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broach, 2012

claim: One of the genes in the Rgt1 pathway was mutated in 8 of the 12 clones.
source: One of the genes in the Rgt1 pathway was mutated in 8 of the 12 clones: SNF3 (3 missense), MTH1 (2 nonsense), and RGT1 (2 nonsense, 1 missense); no clones had two mutations in the pathway.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: No clones had two mutations in the Rgt1 pathway.
source: One of the genes in the Rgt1 pathway was mutated in 8 of the 12 clones: SNF3 (3 missense), MTH1 (2 nonsense), and RGT1 (2 nonsense, 1 missense); no clones had two mutations in the pathway.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: MTH1 loss of function mutations have been selected by others in glucose-limited chemostats.
source: MTH1 loss of function mutations have been selected by others in glucose-limited chemostats (Kao and Sherlock, 2008; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011).

claim: The SNF3 mutations may result in gain of function.
source: On the other hand, because Snf3's activity leads to the induction of glucose-repressed genes, we speculate that the SNF3 mutations may result in gain of function.
evidence: Based on speculation about the function of Snf3

claim: One of the SNF3 mutations (snf3-A231D) lies near a known dominant mutation, SNF3-R229K, that elevates hexose transporter expression.
source: One of our mutations, snf3-A231D, lies near a known dominant mutation, SNF3-R229K (Ozcan et al., 1996), that elevates hexose transporter expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ozcan et al., 1996

claim: The Ras-cAMP pathway regulates cell growth in response to nutrients.
source: The Ras-cAMP pathway regulates cell growth in response to nutrients (Broach, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Broach, 2012

claim: Ira1 and Ira2 both encode GTPase activating proteins that inactivate Ras by stimulating its intrinsic GTPase activity.
source: Ira1 and Ira2 both encode GTPase activating proteins that inactivate Ras by stimulating its intrinsic GTPase activity (Tanaka et al., 1989, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 1989, 1990

claim: IRA1 or IRA2 were mutated in four unrelated evolved clones.
source: IRA1 or IRA2 were mutated in four unrelated evolved clones (3 missense, 1 nonsense).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: Mutations that increase cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity are known to prevent starvation-induced cell cycle arrest.
source: Mutations that increase cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity are known to prevent starvation-induced cell cycle arrest (Matsumoto et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matsumoto et al., 1983

claim: Loss of function mutations in IRA1 and IRA2 will elevate cAMP by increasing Ras activity.
source: By increasing Ras activity, loss of function mutations in IRA1 and IRA2 will elevate cAMP, which may allow cells to grow at lower external sugar concentrations than their ancestors.
evidence: Based on inference from known pathway function

claim: Mutations in four proteins that make up Mediator were found: SIN4, CSE2, MED1, and NUT1.
source: We found mutations in four of the at least 20 proteins that make up Mediator (Myers and Kornberg, 2000): SIN4 (2 missense mutations), CSE2 (1 nonsense mutation), MED1 (1 nonsense mutation), and NUT1 (1 nonsense mutation).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5 and citation to Myers and Kornberg, 2000

claim: Both mutations in SIN4 occurred in residue 128 (G128D, G128S).
source: Both mutations in SIN4 occurred in residue 128 (G128D, G128S) and one, sin4-G128D, was also identified in a screen for suppressors of a deletion in SWI6.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: sin4-G128D was identified in a screen for suppressors of a deletion in SWI6.
source: Both mutations in SIN4 occurred in residue 128 (G128D, G128S) and one, sin4-G128D, was also identified in a screen for suppressors of a deletion in SWI6. Swi6 associates with Swi4 to form SBF (SCB [Swi4-Swi6 cell cycle box] binding factor), a complex that regulates transcription early in the yeast cell cycle (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2005

claim: The hexose transporter gene HXT3 is a known target of SBF.
source: The hexose transporter gene, HXT3, (Iyer et al., 2001) is a known target of SBF and its was strongly elevated (108-fold and 32-fold) in the two clones (EvoClone1 and EvoClone4) carrying SIN4 mutation (Table 2 and 5).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iyer et al., 2001

claim: HXT3 was strongly elevated (108-fold and 32-fold) in the two clones (EvoClone1 and EvoClone4) carrying SIN4 mutation.
source: The hexose transporter gene, HXT3, (Iyer et al., 2001) is a known target of SBF and its was strongly elevated (108-fold and 32-fold) in the two clones (EvoClone1 and EvoClone4) carrying SIN4 mutation (Table 2 and 5).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Tables 2 and 5

claim: The number of hexose transporter gene repeats at the HXT6/7 locus increased from two in the ancestral strain to three in EvoClone7C.
source: The number of hexose transporter gene repeats at the HXT6/7 locus increased from two in the ancestral strain to three in EvoClone7C. This amplification was also present in the backcrossed strain, indicating that it also may have been causal.
evidence: Supported by read depth analysis from whole genome sequencing

claim: Amplification of the HXT6/7 locus has been found in other experimental evolutions.
source: Amplification of the HXT6/7 locus has been found in other experimental evolutions (Brown et al., 1998; Gresham et al., 2008; Kao and Sherlock, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brown et al., 1998; Gresham et al., 2008; Kao and Sherlock, 2008

claim: The morphology and the clump size distribution of the recreated strains are similar to that of the evolved clones.

claim: Both the evolved and recreated clones outcompeted their ancestor in 1–2 passages.
source: Both the evolved and recreated clones outcompeted their ancestor in 1–2 passages (Table 1) showing that they are much fitter on low sucrose.

claim: Both recreated strains were slightly less fit their evolved counterparts.

claim: Both reverted strains (Reverted2 and Reverted9) grew poorly in 1 mM sucrose, mostly existed as single cells, and were quickly outcompeted by the evolved clones.

claim: All five mutations in Recreated2 were strongly selected for.
source: All five mutations in Recreated2 were strongly selected for, six of the eight mutations in Recreated9 were strongly selected for, and one mutation in Recreated9 was moderately selected for, confirming that all but one of the thirteen putative causal mutations were causal for improved growth on low sucrose (Figure 8).

claim: Six of the eight mutations in Recreated9 were strongly selected for.
source: All five mutations in Recreated2 were strongly selected for, six of the eight mutations in Recreated9 were strongly selected for, and one mutation in Recreated9 was moderately selected for, confirming that all but one of the thirteen putative causal mutations were causal for improved growth on low sucrose (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by bulk segregant analysis data shown in Figure 8

claim: One mutation in Recreated9 was moderately selected for.
source: All five mutations in Recreated2 were strongly selected for, six of the eight mutations in Recreated9 were strongly selected for, and one mutation in Recreated9 was moderately selected for, confirming that all but one of the thirteen putative causal mutations were causal for improved growth on low sucrose (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by bulk segregant analysis data shown in Figure 8

claim: All but one of the thirteen putative causal mutations were causal for improved growth on low sucrose.

claim: The eighth mutation in Recreated9, gcn2-I1528L, may be a false positive.
source: We suspect that the eighth mutation in Recreated9, gcn2-I1528L, may be a false positive. claim: The putative causal alleles are both necessary and sufficient to produce the evolved phenotype.
source: In sum, our recreation experiments show that the putative causal alleles, with a single exception, are both necessary and sufficient to produce the evolved phenotype.

claim: Several mutations were selected for in low sucrose but not in low monosaccharide: mutations in MTH1, CSE2, and ACE2 in Recreated2; and in MCK1, IRC8, and GIN4 in Recreated9.

claim: An ace2Δ strain is morphologically similar to EvoClone2.

claim: A mck1-G227Vfs249 irc8-G57V gin4-W19* strain is morphologically similar to EvoClone9.
source: The primary selective force for four of these six mutations is likely to be their ability to produce multicellularity: an ace2Δ strain is morphologically similar to EvoClone2 and a mck1-G227Vfs249 irc8-G57V gin4-W19* strain is morphologically similar to EvoClone9 (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8

claim: An ace2Δ strain outcompetes the ancestor strain in low sucrose but not in low monosaccharide.
source: Each of these two strains also outcompetes the ancestor strain in low sucrose but not in low monosaccharide (Table 1).

claim: Both causal alleles and hitchhiking alleles contribute to the evolved clones' reduced fitness in high glucose.
source: For both EvoClone2 and EvoClone9, the recreated strains performed as well as or better than the evolved clones, but worse than the ancestor, suggesting that both causal alleles and hitchhiking alleles contribute to the evolved clones' reduced fitness in high glucose.
evidence: Based on inference from competition data comparing evolved, recreated, and ancestor strains

claim: The increase in HXT4 expression is a result of the MTH1 loss of function mutation (mth1-H154Tfs156).
source: The increase in HXT4 expression is clearly a result of the MTH1 loss of function mutation (mth1-H154Tfs156): all combinations containing this allele have higher HXT4 expression than those containing the ancestral MTH1 allele.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: SUC2 expression is a complex phenotype under the quantitative control of alleles at several genes.
source: The gradient in SUC2 expression across the allelic combinations indicates that SUC2 expression is a complex phenotype, which is under the quantitative control alleles at several genes.
evidence: Based on inference from RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: The clumpiness in EvoClone2 is caused by the loss of function mutation in ACE2.
source: We also checked the clumpiness of each strain by manual observation using a microscope: the strains with the wild type ACE2 allele were not clumpy, while each strain with ace2-L323* was clumpy. This result confirms that the clumpiness in EvoClone2 is caused by the loss of function mutation in ACE2.
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations of strains with different ACE2 alleles

claim: Combining rational design with experimental evolution can help evaluate hypotheses about evolutionary strategies.
source: Our study shows that combining rational design with experimental evolution can help evaluate hypotheses about evolutionary strategies.
evidence: Based on inference from the overall study design and results

claim: Undifferentiated eukaryotic multicellularity may have existed 2 billion years ago.
source: Indeed, there is suggestive evidence of undifferentiated eukaryotic multicellularity 2 billion years ago (El Albani et al. 2010), but the radiation of more complex multicellularity is not seen for over a billion years later.
evidence: Supported by citation to El Albani et al. 2010

claim: The radiation of more complex multicellularity is not seen for over a billion years after the first evidence of undifferentiated multicellularity.
source: Indeed, there is suggestive evidence of undifferentiated eukaryotic multicellularity 2 billion years ago (El Albani et al. 2010), but the radiation of more complex multicellularity is not seen for over a billion years later.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the fossil record

claim: Unicellular organisms have evolved a combination of three strategies to access nutrients that are digested extracellularly: increasing secretion of an extracellular hydrolase, increasing the import of its products, and forming multicellular clumps.
source: We speculate that unicellular organisms have evolved a combination of three strategies to access nutrients that are digested extracellularly: increasing secretion of an extracellular hydrolase, increasing the import of its products, and forming multicellular clumps.
evidence: Based on speculation from the experimental results

claim: Yeast, when selected for growth in low sucrose media, used a mixture of all three strategies (increased enzyme secretion, increased transporter expression, and multicellular clumps).
source: We have shown that yeast, when selected for growth in low sucrose media, used a mixture of all three strategies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from evolved clones

claim: The combination of laboratory engineering and evolutionary analysis supports the speculation that the sharing of public goods was the initial selection for undifferentiated multicellularity.
source: The combination of laboratory engineering and evolutionary analysis shown here and in our previous work supports the speculation that the sharing of public goods was the initial selection for undifferentiated multicellularity.
evidence: Based on inference from the current study and previous work

claim: For organisms with rigid cell walls like yeast, algae, and bacteria, the target size for mutations in cell separation enzymes and their control circuits will be large, making it easy to evolve undifferentiated multicellularity.
source: For organisms with rigid cell walls like yeast, algae, and bacteria, cells must secrete enzymes to separate mother from daughter after cytokinesis. The target size for mutations in these enzymes and the control circuits that regulate their production will be large, making it easy to evolve undifferentiated multicellularity.
evidence: Based on inference from the biology of cell separation and mutation rates

claim: Lab strains of yeast were selected to be unicellular during their domestication.
source: Although lab strains of yeast were selected to be unicellular during their domestication (Mortimer and Johnston, 1986), the level of clumpiness varies in wild isolates of yeast, and undifferentiated multicellularity may have been recurrently selected for its advantage in harvesting nutrients or for protection from stress (Smukalla et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mortimer and Johnston, 1986; Smukalla et al., 2008

claim: The level of clumpiness varies in wild isolates of yeast.
source: Although lab strains of yeast were selected to be unicellular during their domestication (Mortimer and Johnston, 1986), the level of clumpiness varies in wild isolates of yeast, and undifferentiated multicellularity may have been recurrently selected for its advantage in harvesting nutrients or for protection from stress (Smukalla et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on knowledge of wild yeast populations

claim: Undifferentiated multicellularity may have been recurrently selected for its advantage in harvesting nutrients or for protection from stress.
source: Although lab strains of yeast were selected to be unicellular during their domestication (Mortimer and Johnston, 1986), the level of clumpiness varies in wild isolates of yeast, and undifferentiated multicellularity may have been recurrently selected for its advantage in harvesting nutrients or for protection from stress (Smukalla et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to Smukalla et al., 2008

claim: Organisms without a cell wall would need another innovation, such as cell-adhering cadherins, in order to evolve multicellular clumps.
source: Organisms without a cell wall, such as animal cells, would need another innovation, such as cell-adhering cadherins (Abedin and King, 2008), in order to evolve multicellular clumps.
evidence: Based on inference and citation to Abedin and King, 2008

claim: The effectiveness of clumping as a strategy could be improved if a limited number of cells increase their enzyme secretion.
source: From our data, we speculate that the effectiveness of clumping as a strategy could be improved if a limited number of cells increase their enzyme secretion. Such a simple division of labor may have been the precursor to complex multicellularity in the lineages that lead to animals and other complex multicellular species.
evidence: Based on speculation from the experimental data

claim: A simple division of labor may have been the precursor to complex multicellularity in the lineages that lead to animals and other complex multicellular species.
source: From our data, we speculate that the effectiveness of clumping as a strategy could be improved if a limited number of cells increase their enzyme secretion. Such a simple division of labor may have been the precursor to complex multicellularity in the lineages that lead to animals and other complex multicellular species.
evidence: Based on speculation from the experimental data

claim: A total of 80 putative causal mutations were found in the twelve evolved clones out of 1521 mutations.
source: We found a total of 80 putative causal mutations in the twelve evolved clones out of 1521 mutations, confirming that most mutations are non-causal (Table 5).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing and bulk segregant analysis data shown in Table 5

claim: Most mutations in the evolved clones are non-causal.
source: We found a total of 80 putative causal mutations in the twelve evolved clones out of 1521 mutations, confirming that most mutations are non-causal (Table 5).
evidence: Based on inference from the ratio of causal to total mutations

claim: The 80 putative causal mutations lie in or near 53 genes.
source: Over all 12 clones, the 80 putative causal mutations lie in or near 53 genes.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Table 5

claim: Four genes involved in cell separation (AMN1, CTS1, DSE2, and SCW11) had significantly reduced levels in all 11 clumpy evolved clones.
source: Four genes involved in cell separation, AMN1, CTS1, DSE2, and SCW11, had significantly reduced levels in all 11 clumpy evolved clones, and three other genes implicated in cell separation showed reduced expression in 10 (DSE1, SUN4), or 9 (DSE4) of the clumpy clones.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Table 3

claim: Three other genes implicated in cell separation (DSE1, SUN4, DSE4) showed reduced expression in 10 or 9 of the clumpy clones.
source: Four genes involved in cell separation, AMN1, CTS1, DSE2, and SCW11, had significantly reduced levels in all 11 clumpy evolved clones, and three other genes implicated in cell separation showed reduced expression in 10 (DSE1, SUN4), or 9 (DSE4) of the clumpy clones.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Table 3

claim: These seven genes are not decreased in expression in the non-clumpy evolved clone (EvoClone7B) or the control strain.
source: These seven genes are not decreased in expression in the non-clumpy evolved clone (EvoClone7B) or the control strain.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Table 3

claim: Growth of all the evolved clones depends on secreted invertase.
source: In each case, the evolved clone quickly outcompeted the version that did not secrete invertase (Table 4), demonstrating that growth of all the evolved clones depends on secreted invertase.
evidence: Supported by competition data shown in Table 4

claim: Expression of SUC2 was slightly greater in the suc2-1cyt strain but statistically insignificant over three independent trials.
source: To verify that this growth defect was not due to reduction in invertase expression, we measured, using reverse transcription followed by quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), the SUC2 expression of the two evolved clones (EvoClone2 and EvoClone9) and their suc2-1cyt counterparts grown in 1 mM glucose. In both cases, expression of SUC2 was slightly greater in the suc2-1cyt strain but statistically insignificant over three independent trials.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data

claim: None of the evolved clones had a strong fitness advantage over the ancestor in 1 mM glucose plus 1 mM fructose.
source: First, none of the evolved clones had a strong fitness advantage over the ancestor in 1 mM glucose plus 1 mM fructose, the monosaccharide equivalent of 1 mM sucrose (Table 1) showing that these clones were specifically adapted to sucrose.
evidence: Supported by competition data shown in Table 1

claim: The evolved clones were specifically adapted to sucrose.
source: First, none of the evolved clones had a strong fitness advantage over the ancestor in 1 mM glucose plus 1 mM fructose, the monosaccharide equivalent of 1 mM sucrose (Table 1) showing that these clones were specifically adapted to sucrose.
evidence: Based on inference from competition data in different media

claim: A strain that was engineered to be clumpy (EngClumpy) outcompeted the ancestor in low sucrose, but not low monosaccharide.
source: Second, a strain that was engineered to be clumpy (EngClumpy) outcompeted the ancestor in low sucrose, but not low monosaccharide (Table 1), demonstrating that low sucrose concentrations specifically selects for clumps, reinforcing our earlier findings on engineered multicellularity (Koschwanez et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by competition data shown in Table 1 and citation to Koschwanez et al., 2011

claim: Low sucrose concentrations specifically select for clumps.
source: Second, a strain that was engineered to be clumpy (EngClumpy) outcompeted the ancestor in low sucrose, but not low monosaccharide (Table 1), demonstrating that low sucrose concentrations specifically selects for clumps, reinforcing our earlier findings on engineered multicellularity (Koschwanez et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on inference from competition data and citation to Koschwanez et al., 2011

claim: The alleles that recreate the clumpy morphology are strongly selected for in low sucrose and are not selected for in low monosaccharide.
source: Third, the alleles that recreate the clumpy morphology (ace2-L323* in EvoClone2 and the combination of mck1-G227Vfs249, gin4-W19*, and irc8-G57V in EvoClone9) are strongly selected for in low sucrose and are not selected for in low monosaccharide (Figure 8 and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by bulk segregant analysis data shown in Figure 8 and Table 1

claim: More efficient sucrose utilization, rather than some other phenotype, selected for the clumpy phenotype.
source: Because the starting pool of segregants and the selection protocol was identical in both media, this result shows that more efficient sucrose utilization, rather than some other phenotype, selected for the clumpy phenotype.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental design and results

claim: Most (10 out of 12) of the evolved clones had increased invertase expression.
source: Most (10 out of 12) of the evolved clones had increased invertase expression, even though the strain we had engineered to have high invertase expression had only a small advantage over a wild-type strain (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Table 2

claim: The strain engineered to have high invertase expression had only a small advantage over a wild-type strain.
source: Most (10 out of 12) of the evolved clones had increased invertase expression, even though the strain we had engineered to have high invertase expression had only a small advantage over a wild-type strain (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by competition data shown in Table 1

claim: Increasing invertase expression makes sense in conjunction with multicellularity and elevated monosaccharide import.
source: But high invertase expression makes sense in conjunction with the other two strategies we observed, multicellularity and elevated monosaccharide import.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined effects of multiple strategies

claim: In a clump, multiple cells share a larger unstirred volume and have preferential access to the monosaccharides their neighbors release.
source: In a clump, multiple cells share a larger unstirred volume and have preferential access to the monosaccharides their neighbors release (Koschwanez et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koschwanez et al., 2011

claim: Increasing invertase expression will increase the rate of sucrose hydrolysis.
source: Increasing invertase expression will increase the rate of sucrose hydrolysis, and making more hexose transporters will increase the fraction of the monosaccharides that are imported rather than escaping to the bulk medium.
evidence: Based on inference from enzyme kinetics

claim: Making more hexose transporters will increase the fraction of the monosaccharides that are imported rather than escaping to the bulk medium.
source: Increasing invertase expression will increase the rate of sucrose hydrolysis, and making more hexose transporters will increase the fraction of the monosaccharides that are imported rather than escaping to the bulk medium.
evidence: Based on inference from transporter function

claim: Increasing invertase expression, making cell clumps, and making more hexose transporters will act together to increase fitness on low sucrose.
source: Thus we expect that increasing invertase expression, making cell clumps, and making more hexose transporters will act together to increase fitness on low sucrose.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined effects of multiple strategies

claim: Low extracellular glucose induces the expression of both high affinity hexose transporters and invertase.
source: Because low extracellular glucose induces the expression of both high affinity hexose transporters and invertase, it is likely that single mutations can increase levels of both types of proteins.
evidence: Based on knowledge of glucose regulation in yeast

claim: Single mutations can likely increase levels of both hexose transporters and invertase.
source: Because low extracellular glucose induces the expression of both high affinity hexose transporters and invertase, it is likely that single mutations can increase levels of both types of proteins.
evidence: Based on inference from glucose regulation

claim: Clumpiness may indirectly elevate invertase expression because concentrating the cells in space collectively raises the local glucose concentration.
source: In addition, clumpiness may indirectly elevate invertase expression: because secreted invertase expression peaks at roughly 0.5 mM external glucose (Koschwanez et al., 2011), clumps may increase invertase expression because concentrating the cells in space collectively raises the local glucose concentration.
evidence: Based on speculation and citation to Koschwanez et al., 2011

claim: Secreted invertase expression peaks at roughly 0.5 mM external glucose.
source: In addition, clumpiness may indirectly elevate invertase expression: because secreted invertase expression peaks at roughly 0.5 mM external glucose (Koschwanez et al., 2011), clumps may increase invertase expression because concentrating the cells in space collectively raises the local glucose concentration.
evidence: Supported by citation to Koschwanez et al., 2011
